sources.title: Evaluación multi-amenaza en cuatro zonas del Uruguay, considerando escenarios de cambio climático. Etapa C: Informe preliminar, Producto 3
sources.organization: Factor CO2 for Uruguay's NAP Ciudades project, with DINAGUA and DINAMA counterparts
sources.temporal_coverage: Report delivered 22 April 2020; local vulnerability indicators use 2011 census data; climate projections cover 2020–2044 and 2045–2099.
sources.methodology: Preliminary multi-hazard GIS combines climate scenarios, urban exposure, census sensitivity and qualitative adaptation capacity.
sources.limitations: Preliminary; local validation pending. Adaptation capacity was not quantified.

sources.title: Uruguay: 2024 Article IV Consultation—Staff Report, IMF Country Report No. 24/215
sources.temporal_coverage: Article IV report completed 14 June 2024; drought analysis includes 2022Q4–2023Q2 and the SMDI reference series 2000–2023.
sources.methodology: IMF macro study uses soil-moisture data, SVAR and DSGE models.
sources.limitations: Weather shocks are not anthropogenic attribution; relocation passage gives no locations.

sources.title: Informe de situación por inundaciones - Fin de la emergencia (08/01/24)
sources.temporal_coverage: Closeout of the 80-day Uruguay River flood emergency of October 2023–January 2024.
sources.methodology: National emergency situation report drawing on SINAE, DINAGUA, meteorological and departmental response information.
sources.limitations: Event-specific official reporting; it does not attribute the flood to long-term anthropogenic climate change.

sources.title: Balance anual de emergencias: los eventos adversos más significativos de 2024
sources.temporal_coverage: Annual emergency balance for 2024, published 10 January 2025.
sources.methodology: SINAE annual summary of hydrometeorological emergencies with affected-people and housing tables by event and department.
sources.limitations: This event inventory reports impacts, not anthropogenic attribution; its aggregate prose conflicts with the table total, so claims use the flood-specific table row or event-specific figures only.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.7–8 (printed pp.5–6), objectives and study coverage.
claims.paraphrase: Study covers Juan Lacaze, Rivera, Canelones and Arroyo Pantanoso in Montevideo to identify urban risk and priority zones.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.19–20 (printed pp.17–18), vulnerability index inputs.
claims.paraphrase: 2011 census-block indicators include age under 15 or over 65, severe disability, crowding, insecure tenure, substandard housing, lack of piped water or sanitation, and informal settlements.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.22–23 (printed pp.20–21), hazard-specific vulnerability criteria.
claims.paraphrase: Heat vulnerability combines hazard with age, disability, water access and crowding; flood with crowding, sanitation, insecure tenure and informal settlements.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.19 (printed p.16), sewer-network exposure indicator.
claims.paraphrase: Juan Lacaze had no sewer network in study data; lower coverage counted as higher hydrometeorological exposure.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.27 (printed p.24), adaptation-capacity section.
claims.paraphrase: Local capacity review considers risk maps, risk-informed plans, early warning and government/community coordination.
claims.limitations: Qualitative; not in the vulnerability index.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.11 and 25–27 (printed pp.8 and 22–24), projection periods and risk-map caveat.
claims.paraphrase: Maps project hazards to 2044 and 2099; flood and drainage areas remain unchanged without hydrological modeling.
claims.scenario: SSP/CMIP6; flood/drainage projections not hydrologically recalculated.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.42 (printed p.38), Annex I paragraphs 1–3 and SMDI data note.
claims.paraphrase: The 2022Q4–2023Q2 drought cut agricultural output 25% year on year; analysis focuses on seven named agriculture departments.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.41 (printed p.37), Annex I paragraph 1.
claims.paraphrase: Rain and floods forced vulnerable groups to relocate: about 3% of the population in 2015–19, with livelihood impacts.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Rain/floods -> relocation and livelihood impacts; p.37.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.42 (printed p.38), Annex I paragraph 4 and Figure 1 note.
claims.paraphrase: One-SD drought shock modeled: agriculture -0.1% at impact; GDP -0.3% after three quarters; agricultural effects persist 2 years (SVAR) to 5 (DSGE).
claims.scenario: One-SD soil-moisture deficit in SVAR/DSGE; not an emissions scenario.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.41 (printed p.37), Annex I paragraph 2.
claims.paraphrase: Authorities modeled drought, excess-rainfall and coastal-flood fiscal impacts for budget integration after recurring responses pressured fiscal space.

claims.locator: Official page, event summary and evolution, paragraphs on the 80-day emergency and peak displacement.
claims.paraphrase: The October 2023–January 2024 Uruguay River flood affected Artigas, Cerro Largo, Paysandú, Salto and Tacuarembó; peak displacement was 3,511 people, over 90% self-evacuated, with the largest counts in Paysandú, Salto and Artigas.
claims.limitations: Event report links the flood to heavy basin rainfall and El Niño conditions, not long-term anthropogenic climate change.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Uruguay River flooding -> evacuation and self-evacuation; official page, event summary, paragraphs on duration and peak displacement.

claims.locator: Official page, local impact sections for Paysandú and Salto, paragraphs naming most affected zones.
claims.paraphrase: In Paysandú, Diagonal San Félix, the waterfront, Unión Portuaria and the racetrack vicinity were among the hardest-hit areas; in Salto, the waterfront, Arenitas Blancas and Parque Harriague were most affected.
claims.limitations: The report identifies affected locations but gives no site-level resident or housing denominators.

claims.locator: Official page, Actions de respuesta section, paragraphs on SATI, protocol and departmental preparation.
claims.paraphrase: The lower Uruguay River SATI combines meteorological and hydrological forecasts; early warning enabled evacuation before floodwater reached homes, while departmental committees prepared response resources and evacuation centers.
claims.limitations: The report describes one event and response; it does not evaluate protection outcomes for all households.

claims.locator: Official page, Eventos hidrometeorológicos table, flood row and department summaries.
claims.paraphrase: SINAE's 2024 table attributes 13,682 affected people and 5,090 affected homes to 40 floods; flood-row counts include 7,252 women, 6,430 men, 9,065 adults and 4,617 minors. Durazno, San José, Paysandú and Florida had the most people affected overall.
claims.limitations: The narrative aggregate conflicts with the table total; figures here are only the flood-specific table row and the separate department ranking.

claims.locator: Official page, paragraphs on the 8 March–5 April 2024 flood emergency.
claims.paraphrase: March rainfall totals doubled usual monthly averages; flooding reached Santa Lucía and 25 de Agosto in Canelones and Florida, places described as historically unaffected, and displaced 8,268 people across 13 departments.
claims.limitations: Report associates flooding with unusually high rainfall; it does not attribute the event to anthropogenic climate change.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Heavy rainfall -> flooding and displacement across 13 departments; official page, 8 March–5 April event paragraphs.

search_audit.query: Uruguay climate vulnerability drought municipalities departments agriculture water vulnerable groups official report PDF
search_audit.outcome: Opened the complete official urban multi-hazard assessment and IMF drought annex; found local vulnerability indicators for four named urban areas and drought exposure across named departments.

search_audit.query: Uruguay climate change conflict social tensions drought water insecurity migration report official primary
search_audit.outcome: IMF and SINAE directly document flood-linked relocation and livelihood effects; no reviewed primary passage establishes a climate-to-violent-conflict or criminal-insecurity pathway.

search_audit.query: Uruguay violence insecurity disaster climate adaptation disruption drought official report
search_audit.outcome: Searches did not identify a primary source showing violence or insecurity disrupting climate adaptation, early warning or disaster response; no reverse pathway is asserted.

search_audit.query: Uruguay climate adaptation resilience capacity early warning drought water government UNDP report official PDF
search_audit.outcome: The urban assessment reviews risk mapping and planning capacity; SINAE reports that the SATI warning and interagency protocol enabled evacuation before floodwater reached homes.

gaps: Reviewed primary reports document climate and hydrometeorological impacts, relocation, livelihood losses and preparedness but do not establish a link to armed conflict, political violence, crime or social unrest.

No primary source was identified in this search showing insecurity or violence obstructing climate adaptation, early warning or disaster response; this is a search gap, not evidence that such effects never occur.

The four-city vulnerability assessment is preliminary, relies on 2011 census indicators and did not quantitatively integrate adaptation capacity; its flood projections lack hydrological recalculation.
The IMF relocation estimate is national and does not identify the affected locations; SINAE provides named event locations but limited demographic, tenure or protection detail at site level.
SINAE's 2024 annual page has an inconsistent hydrometeorological aggregate in prose and its table total; claims use only the flood-specific table row or event-specific reported counts.
